title: Global wealth expanded rapidly while median experience, regional position, and ownership remained sharply uneven
source_unit: UBS Global Wealth Report 2026, seventeenth edition, using estimated personal wealth across 56 key markets
geography: 56 markets estimated by UBS to represent over 92% of global wealth, with regional, country, wealth-band, and high-net-worth comparisons

denominator.unit: markets covered by UBS wealth estimates, representing over 92% of global wealth

total_wealth_growth.value: Total personal wealth rose 10.8% in 2025 in U.S.-dollar terms
total_wealth_growth.unit: annual percentage change in estimated personal wealth

median_average_divergence.value: Average wealth rose while median wealth declined in most markets

millionaire_growth.value: The global millionaire population expanded by 1.5%, nearly one million people, or more than 2,680 per day

interpretation.value: Aggregate wealth growth can coexist with a weaker typical household position, making distribution—not only growth—the politically salient signal

observations.method: UBS models personal wealth using OECD, IMF, UN, World Bank, national-statistics, and market data across 56 markets; wealth includes financial and non-financial assets net of debt.
observations.uncertainty: The report is UBS analysis and marketing material, not a household panel or official wealth census. Currency conversion, asset-price movements, modelling, market selection, and methodology changes affect the estimates; comparisons across editions are not always possible.
observations.subgroup: Adults by wealth band, country, region, median versus average position, and high-net-worth status; the sample is not a representative survey of lived financial security.
observations.counterinterpretation: Median wealth can fall because of exchange rates, population composition, debt normalization, or asset-price concentration without a universal decline in living standards; millionaire counts do not measure wellbeing or social power directly.

observations.period: 2020–2025; real wealth per adult and regional divergence

denominator.unit: markets in the UBS longitudinal wealth sample

average_wealth_range.value: Real average wealth per adult rose more than 55% in South Korea since 2020, while it declined in 15 markets, including the United Kingdom by 23.2%

median_wealth_range.value: Fewer than half of the markets had higher median wealth per adult in 2025 than in 2020, while median wealth declined by more than 10% in 20 markets

regional_share.value: The Americas held about 40.6% of sample wealth, EMEA 26.6%, and Asia-Pacific 32.8% in 2025
regional_share.unit: share of estimated wealth in UBS sample

interpretation.value: Wealth mobility is geographically uneven and the median-versus-average split is a better signal of broad-based security than headline asset appreciation

observations.method: UBS compares inflation-adjusted wealth per adult in local currency over 2020–2025 and reports regional shares in U.S.-dollar terms.
observations.uncertainty: The measures use different currencies and metrics; local-real and U.S.-dollar comparisons answer different questions. Exchange rates, inflation, population change, and asset composition can substantially alter rankings.
observations.subgroup: Markets and regions with different currencies, asset ownership, housing markets, debt structures, and demographic trends.
observations.counterinterpretation: Regional wealth-share changes may reflect currency appreciation rather than real redistribution of assets, and national averages conceal within-country inequality.

denominator.unit: markets in the UBS wealth-pyramid model

lowest_band.value: The share of the global population with net assets below USD 10,000 fell from almost three-quarters in 2000 to just over 41% at the end of 2025
lowest_band.unit: share of modeled global adult population

middle_bands.value: The USD 10,000–100,000 wealth band expanded substantially, while the two highest bands more than doubled their membership

debt_normalization.value: Household debt rose in 2025 after shrinking in 2024, returning toward more normal historical levels

interpretation.value: A larger middle wealth population can coexist with stronger concentration and rising debt, creating a layered rather than simply upward mobility story

observations.method: The report models movement across net-wealth bands over time and separates financial and non-financial assets from household debt.
observations.uncertainty: Wealth-band thresholds are nominal and modelled; inflation adjustment changes the interpretation, and the report notes that methodological updates and exchange rates complicate historical comparisons.
observations.subgroup: Adults below USD 10,000, middle wealth bands, millionaires, billionaires, debt holders, and markets with different asset and liability structures.
observations.counterinterpretation: Movement into a higher nominal wealth band may not mean increased real security if housing, education, health, or debt costs rise faster than assets; a shrinking lowest band does not establish equal opportunity.

denominator.unit: markets in the UBS wealth-composition analysis; art sub-analysis draws on 3,100 HNWIs in 10 markets

liquid_wealth.value: Liquid assets rose as a share of total net wealth over the past 10–15 years; the United States was reported at roughly 47% liquid wealth in 2025
liquid_wealth.unit: share of total personal net wealth

art_allocation.value: HNWIs in the cited Art Basel and UBS survey held an average 20% of wealth in art in 2025
art_allocation.unit: share of wealth among surveyed HNWIs

meaning_and_value.value: The report presents art as simultaneously a personal, social, philanthropic, identity-bearing, and wealth-preservation asset

interpretation.value: Wealth is not only purchasing power: it structures liquidity, inheritance, cultural identity, and the ability to preserve meaning-bearing assets

observations.method: UBS combines modeled wealth composition with a cited Art Basel and UBS survey of 3,100 HNWIs across 10 markets.
observations.uncertainty: The HNWI art survey is not representative of the general population, and the wealth-composition estimates depend on asset classification, valuation, ownership structures, and country data.
observations.subgroup: High-net-worth individuals, direct equity holders, homeowners, pension savers, art collectors, and adults with different access to liquid and illiquid assets.
observations.counterinterpretation: Art holdings may be concentrated and illiquid, so their cultural meaning does not imply broad economic resilience; rising liquid wealth shares can also reflect financialization rather than more usable household security.

related_sources.claim: Official 46-page Global Wealth Report 2026 PDF containing the global-level, distribution, wealth-dynamics, and wealth-snapshot findings.

boundary: This record adds a global wealth, ownership, mobility, debt, liquidity, and cultural-asset layer. It does not provide respondent-level data, a representative household panel, a causal inequality estimate, or a complete account of public wealth, informal assets, unpaid care, or lived financial security; UBS estimates and high-net-worth survey evidence carry institutional and sampling limits.
